newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - Iraq forging southerly path.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - Iraq forging southerly path.

text.p: Iraqi news was seen forging a southerly path for U.S. crude oil prices this week, with a waning hurricane and Colombian developments compounding the downward pressure, analysts and traders said on Monday.
The United Nations in Baghdad on Monday said Iraq had submitted a new aid distribution plan to U.N. headquarters in New York, nudging the resumption of limited oil exports closer to fruition.
The U.N. is expected to take about a week to give the plan final approval, paving the way for Baghdad to submit a new pricing formula for renewed sales.
Cash West Texas Intermediate/Cushing was running around $19.10-20 a barrel at midday, in line with August light sweet crude on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX).
The front-month NYMEX contract was trading at $19.16 a barrel at 1614 GMT/1214 EDT, down 11 cents from Friday's settlement.
The August contract expires on Tuesday.
The sometimes unpredicable record of the U.N. oil-for-food program led to some lingering skepticism as to the exact timing of renewed sales.

"(The crude price) hinges on the status of the distribution plan. The assumption is that it's a rubber-stamp process...but we shouldn't necessarily make that assumption," said William Brown, president of W.H. Brown & Co in New York.
Another analyst conceded that while the market remains in a bearish mode, the absence of Iraqi barrels is keeping the physical balance tight.

"Things are holding in, this Iraqi crude shortage is going to keep things tight. Buyers will probably hold off as much as possible until they see some supply," said Warren Tashneck, vice president and manager of FIMAT USA, Inc in Houston.
Tashneck said September WTI should remain in a range of between $18.30-40 and $20.50 a barrel.
A Texas trader added that now that Hurricane Danny in the Gulf of Mexico has passed, both outright and grade prices would likely soften, especially for sweet crude values.

Danny has been downgraded to a tropical depression and was dying slowly, after causing no damage to Gulf oil facilities. Refinery operations in Louisiana and Mississippi have started the process of returning to normal operating levels.
Chevron's 295,000 barrel per day (bpd) Pascagoula, Mississippi refinery was operational again Monday morning, along with the Louisiana Offshore Oil Port (LOOP), BP, Mobil and Texaco facilities.

During the later stages of last week's action, Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James ran higher on fears oil production and assorted facilities would suffer from the storm. LLS sold at a peak of 35 cents over the August benchmark, but faded on Friday and early Monday to only a 20-cent premium.

Sour grades had found some support on word Colombian state oil company Ecopetrol maintained force majeure on Cao Limn exports from the Caribbean terminal of Coveas. The emergency, declared after repeated bombings of the Cao Limn-Coveas pipeline by leftist rebels, had lifted West Texas Sour/Midland prices to only a $1.00 discount to WTI.

But WTS moved some 20 cents off that plateau late last week after repairs were made to the crude artery and field operator Occidental resumed Cao Limn production and lifted force majeure on the field.
Ecopetrol was expected to release a new Cao Limn export schedule late on Monday, possibly coinciding with the lifting of force majeure on loadings.
